comments.author: @jackurbani5851
comments.text:
I always thought that all of the peninsula south of the Chesapeake-Delaware Canal should all be Delaware (or DELMARVA) 
The Chesapeake & Delaware Canal effectively cuts the Delmarva Peninsula into two distinct pieces. An island. 

If you were designing state boundaries around physical geography and transportation corridors rather than colonial-era charters, you could argue:
Everything south of the canal forms one coherent peninsula: Delaware's lower counties, Maryland's Eastern Shore, and Virginia's Eastern Shore.
Everything north of the canal is economically and culturally tied to the Philadelphia region and Pennsylvania's interior.

From an urban-planning perspective, the canal is almost a perfect dividing line: north of it you enter the Philadelphia metropolitan sphere, while south of it you move into the distinctly coastal, agricultural, and resort-oriented culture of Delmarva. The geography arguably makes more sense than the existing state lines.

The Erie Triangle is one of the best examples of how states were willing to stretch boundaries to gain access to strategically important geography.

Simple 🤩

comments.text:
Sorry, Geoff. You need to issue a correction. 
The Ebright Azimuth sign itself, which was erected in collaboration/verification with the US Geological Survey, indicates the elevation of the Ebright Azimuth (on Ebright Road, northern New Castle County, Delaware, very close to the Pennsylvania border) as 447.85 feet (136.50 meters) above sea level. 
"Ebright Azimuth is the official name of Delaware's state highpoint. Although it might not be a traditional peak and isn't a primary destination for peak baggers, it holds significance as one of the 50 State Highpoints. Ebright Azimuth stands at an elevation of 448 feet, making it the second-lowest state highpoint in the United States, just about 100 feet higher than Florida's Britton Hill." - US Highpoint Guide, searchable online. 

Trust me, as a Delaware citizen, I would LOVE the highest point in our state to be the official lowest in the lower 48 - which is a distinction we don't need, when you think about it, because surely Alaska and Hawaii have higher points, so we should simply say, "The lowest in ANY state, period."  But that distinction does indeed belong to Florida.
